questions.question: Why does `CREATE TABLE ... PRIMARY KEY (id) ... PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS (created_at)` fail?
options: RANGE COLUMNS does not support DATETIME
Partitioned tables cannot have an AUTO_INCREMENT column
Every unique key, including the primary key, must include all columns of the partitioning expression
The primary key must be the first column of the table
questions.explanation: MySQL enforces uniqueness only within a partition, so unique keys must contain the partition column. PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at) works.

questions.question: A table is partitioned monthly by `created_at`. Which query will EXPLAIN show touching only one partition?
options: SELECT * FROM orders_p WHERE created_at >= '2025-02-01' AND created_at < '2025-03-01'
SELECT * FROM orders_p WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025 AND MONTH(created_at) = 2
questions.explanation: Pruning needs a direct constraint on the partition column. Filtering on other columns or on functions of the column checks every partition.

questions.question: What is the strongest practical reason to partition a large orders table by month?
options: It lets the table use more CPU cores across multiple servers
Queries on any column automatically become faster
Old data can be removed instantly with DROP PARTITION instead of a huge, log-heavy DELETE
questions.explanation: DROP PARTITION is a metadata operation that avoids massive undo/redo, locking and replication lag. Partitioning does not add server capacity or speed up unrelated queries.

questions.question: For a sharded e-commerce database, why is `customer_id` usually a better shard key than `created_at`?
options: customer_id keeps a customer's orders on one shard and spreads writes evenly, while created_at sends all new writes to the latest shard
questions.explanation: A good shard key has high cardinality, spreads load and keeps a request's rows together. Time-based keys create a write hotspot on the newest shard.
